purpose: Independent smoke-test evaluation of Phase 4 Lesson Reconciliation quality. No prior scores are included.

lesson.title: Word2Vec - Aplicação utilizando Redes Neurais
lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é aplicar o conceito de rede neurais apresentados nos encontros anteriores em conjunto com o Word2Vec para construção de aplicações.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Euclidean Distance as a Similarity Measure
before_phase4_candidates.description: Euclidean distance can be used to quantify how similar two vectors are in a vector space; smaller distance indicates greater similarity.
coverage_criteria: Calculate Euclidean distance between two 2D points given coordinates.
Explain that closer points have smaller Euclidean distance.
Given a set of vectors, identify which one is closest to a target using Euclidean distance.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

anchors.locator: Animal similarity and simple linear algebra

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces Euclidean distance in the animal space example, provides Python code to compute it, and uses it to find similar animals (capybara vs panda).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a fundamental mathematical building block for many similarity-based operations with word vectors. It is small enough to test with simple computation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Nearest Neighbor Search in Vector Space
before_phase4_candidates.description: Given a vector space and a query vector, the closest neighbors can be found by computing distances to all items and selecting the smallest ones.
coverage_criteria: Describe the process of scanning all vectors to find the closest one.
Explain why naive nearest neighbor search is inefficient for large spaces.
Identify that the closest() function in the source implements this by sorting by distance.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates a closest() function that finds the ten closest color names to a given RGB value, and mentions scalability issues and alternatives like kdtree or Annoy.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept isolates the basic algorithm for nearest neighbor, a core operation in vector-based retrieval, without diving into optimized indexing structures.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Vector Arithmetic Operations
before_phase4_candidates.description: Vectors can be added, subtracted, and averaged component-wise, enabling combination and comparison of concepts represented as vectors.
coverage_criteria: Add two vectors by summing corresponding components.
Subtract one vector from another to find the difference.
Compute the mean of a list of vectors.
Explain how the mean vector represents the 'center' of a set of vectors.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides functions addv, subtractv, meanv in Python code within the color vectors section and uses them for color arithmetic, demonstrating how vector operations correspond to combining colors.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The concept covers basic vector algebra operations that are essential for later analogies and sentence averaging, and is testable with simple component-wise calculations.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Analogies through Vector Differences
before_phase4_candidates.description: Analogies can be solved by subtracting the vector of one word from another and adding the difference to a third word's vector, e.g., 'pink is to red as X is to blue'.
coverage_criteria: Given vectors for 'pink', 'red', and 'blue', compute the vector for X that satisfies 'pink - red = X - blue'.
Explain that the difference vector captures the relationship between two words.
Provide an example of an analogy derived from a vector space.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

anchors.locator: Animal similarity and simple linear algebra

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source explicitly demonstrates analogies with color vectors (pink:red::?:blue) and with animal vectors (tarantula:hamster::chicken:kitten), showing that vector differences can model relational similarity.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific application of vector arithmetic that is central to word vector 'magic'; it is a single skill that can be tested with a small computation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Distributional Hypothesis of Meaning
before_phase4_candidates.description: The distributional hypothesis states that words with similar meanings occur in similar contexts; a word's meaning can be inferred from the company it keeps.
coverage_criteria: State the distributional hypothesis.
Given example sentences, identify words that are likely semantically related based on shared contexts.
Explain why 'hot' and 'cold' might be considered similar under this hypothesis despite being antonyms.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces the Distributional Hypothesis with a clear example (cold/warm/hot/cool and yesterday/today/tomorrow/Tuesday) and states that words with similar distributions have similar meanings.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a fundamental theoretical concept that underpins all count-based and predictive word vector methods; it is a single claim that can be tested by having students identify context-based relationships.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word Vectors from Co-occurrence Counts
before_phase4_candidates.description: Word vectors can be constructed by counting how often each word appears in each possible context (e.g., neighboring words), forming a high-dimensional vector per word.
coverage_criteria: Explain how a co-occurrence matrix is built from a text corpus.
Given a small corpus, construct a simple co-occurrence matrix.
Identify that the resulting vector for a word reflects its distributional context.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source walks through creating a spreadsheet from a Dickens sentence, counting word contexts, and explaining that the counts form word vectors, with 'best' and 'worst' having identical vectors because they appear in the same context.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept introduces the concrete method of turning text into vectors, a key step in understanding word embeddings; it is small enough to test with a simple example.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Dimensionality Reduction for Word Vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: High-dimensional word vectors from co-occurrence counts often contain redundant information; dimensionality reduction techniques (like SVD) can compress them into a smaller number of meaningful dimensions.
coverage_criteria: Explain why raw co-occurrence vectors can be too high-dimensional.
Name dimensionality reduction as a solution.
State that typical word vectors have 100-300 dimensions after reduction.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source discusses that many dimensions are superfluous and can be eliminated or combined via dimensionality reduction, mentioning that count-based vectors often use 100-300 dimensions.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept bridges the gap between raw counts and practical word embeddings; it is a single technique that can be tested by asking why reduction is needed and what dimensions are typical.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Pre-trained GloVe Word Vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation) is a set of pre-trained 300-dimensional word vectors available in spaCy, providing a ready-to-use semantic space for English.
coverage_criteria: State that GloVe vectors are 300-dimensional and pre-trained.
Identify that GloVe vectors are included in spaCy's 'en' model.
Explain that using pre-trained vectors saves the effort of training on a corpus.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source introduces GloVe as a downloadable database of pre-trained vectors from Stanford, included with spaCy, and states they will be used for the rest of the tutorial.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical resource concept, informing students that they can leverage existing vectors; it's small and testable with factual recall.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Cosine Similarity for High-Dimensional Vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, providing a useful similarity metric for high-dimensional spaces where Euclidean distance may be less informative.
coverage_criteria: Define cosine similarity formula.
Explain that cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1, with 1 meaning identical direction.
Compare and contrast cosine similarity with Euclidean distance.
Given two vectors, compute cosine similarity (using a formula or Python).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

anchors.locator: Cosine similarity and finding closest neighbors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source provides a cosine() function implementation and uses it to verify that 'dog' and 'puppy' are more similar than 'trousers' and 'octopus', explaining it is more suited to high-dimensional spaces.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Cosine similarity is a specific alternative metric that is essential for working with word vectors; it's a small, well-defined concept.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word Vector Arithmetic with Pre-trained Embeddings
before_phase4_candidates.description: Arithmetic on GloVe word vectors can reveal meaningful semantic relationships, e.g., 'water' + 'frozen' yields 'ice', and 'wine' - 'alcohol' yields words like 'dinner'.
coverage_criteria: Perform vector addition or subtraction with GloVe vectors (hypothetically) and interpret results.
Explain that such arithmetic reflects learned semantic relationships from training data.
Given example arithmetic, predict plausible results based on semantic intuition.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

anchors.locator: Fun with spaCy, Dracula, and vector arithmetic

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source demonstrates several examples: 'wine' - 'alcohol' returns food-related words, 'water' + 'frozen' returns 'ice', 'blue' - 'sky' + 'grass' returns 'green', showing that pre-trained vectors encode relationships.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical skill demonstrating the 'magic' of word vectors, combining vector arithmetic and pre-trained embeddings in a testable way.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Sentence Similarity via Averaged Word Vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: A sentence vector can be obtained by averaging the word vectors of its constituent words, and this can be used to find semantically similar sentences in a corpus.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to compute a sentence vector from word vectors.
Compute the average of multiple word vectors (component-wise).
Describe that cosine similarity between sentence vectors can measure sentence similarity.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Understanding word vectors

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The source defines a sentvec() function that averages word vectors of a sentence, then uses it with spacy_closest_sent() to find sentences in Dracula similar to a query, yielding plausible results.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific technique for extending word vectors to longer texts, small enough to test by having students compute a mean and interpret similarity.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Gensim library for topic modeling and NLP
before_phase4_candidates.description: Gensim is an open-source Python library originally developed for topic modeling, providing models and utilities for unsupervised text analysis including Word2Vec and preprocessing.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that Gensim is a Python library for NLP, mention its origin in topic modeling, and name at least two of its functionalities (e.g., Word2Vec, preprocessing, dictionary creation).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The chapter introduces Gensim as a tool for topic modeling and highlights its use in NLP, starting from page 189.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concept covers the library's identity and purpose; assessable in a few questions about its role and capabilities.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Text preprocessing with gensim.utils.simple_preprocess()
before_phase4_candidates.description: The function simple_preprocess() tokenizes a document, optionally removing accents and filtering tokens by minimum and maximum length.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to call simple_preprocess() on a string, specifying parameters deacc, min_len, max_len, and explain what each does.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 1 – Definição de um corpus e pré-processamento, page 193

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 1 on pages 192-193 demonstrates using simple_preprocess with deacc and min_len, and the surrounding text explains the parameters.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Single function with a clear interface; can be checked with a coding exercise and explanation of parameters.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Tokenization with gensim.utils.tokenize()
before_phase4_candidates.description: The gensim.utils.tokenize() function performs low-level tokenization, internally called by simple_preprocess(), and can be used directly for tokenizing words.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that tokenize() splits text into tokens and is less feature-rich than simple_preprocess, and can write a call to tokenize().
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Page 194 mentions tokenize() as an alternative for word tokenization, stating it is called internally by simple_preprocess.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Narrow concept focusing on one utility function; can be assessed with a simple usage question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Building a vocabulary with gensim.corpora.Dictionary()
before_phase4_candidates.description: gensim.corpora.Dictionary creates a mapping between tokens and integer IDs from preprocessed documents, acting as the model's vocabulary.
coverage_criteria: Given a list of tokenized documents, student can instantiate a Dictionary and explain its purpose in encoding words.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 2 – Vocabulário criado a partir dos documentos tokenizados e tratados, page 194

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 2 on pages 194-195 uses corpDict to build a vocabulary from preprocessed documents, and the text describes its necessity before model creation.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concept covers a single class and its main role; easily testable with a code snippet and brief explanation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Dense versus sparse vector representations
before_phase4_candidates.description: Documents can be represented as vectors; dense vectors have all dimensions known and directly related, while sparse vectors have many unknown dimensions treated as zero.
coverage_criteria: Student can define dense and sparse vectors and give an example of when each would be used in text representation.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Page 195 explicitly contrasts dense and sparse vectors, defining each and stating that unknown dimensions in sparse vectors are zero.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concept is a foundational distinction in vector representations; assessable with a definition and simple scenario.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Training a Word2Vec model with gensim.models.Word2Vec()
before_phase4_candidates.description: The Word2Vec class in Gensim trains word embeddings on a preprocessed corpus using continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) or skip-gram with options for hierarchical softmax or negative sampling.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to instantiate Word2Vec with a list of tokenized sentences, specify min_count and size, and explain that the model learns vector representations.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 3 – Treinamento de um modelo de word2vec, page 196

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 3 on page 196 trains a Word2Vec model and the surrounding text explains the usage and parameters.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Covers the central API for Word2Vec training; can be assessed with a coding task and a question on basic parameters.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec training parameters
before_phase4_candidates.description: Key parameters for gensim.models.Word2Vec() include min_count, size, sg (0: skip-gram, 1: CBOW), window, hs (hierarchical softmax), negative (negative sampling), alpha (learning rate), seed, and corpus_file.
coverage_criteria: Student can list at least four training parameters and explain how they affect the training process.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Pages 196-198 detail many parameters for Word2Vec, explaining each in the context of training.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Combines multiple related parameters into a single concept about model configuration; can be tested with a matching or short-answer question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Saving and loading Word2Vec models
before_phase4_candidates.description: Gensim Word2Vec models can be saved to disk using save() and reloaded later with load(), facilitating reuse of trained embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to save a trained model to a file and load it back using gensim's save and load methods.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 4 – Armazenando um modelo de word2vec, page 198

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 4 (page 198-199) saves a model and Example 5 (page 199) loads it, explicitly showing the workflow.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Narrow concept around two functions; easily checked with code completion.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using pre-trained word embeddings with gensim.downloader
before_phase4_candidates.description: The gensim.downloader module allows loading publicly available pre-trained models like word2vec-google-news-300, which provides high-quality embeddings for downstream tasks.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to load a pre-trained model using gensim.downloader.load() and cite an example such as 'word2vec-google-news-300'.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 6 – Carregando um modelo pré-treinado, page 200

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 6 on page 200 demonstrates loading a pre-trained model, and the text explains the benefits of using large pre-trained embeddings.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Single function with a clear purpose; testable with a code snippet and recognition of common models.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Finding similar words with model.similar_by_word()
before_phase4_candidates.description: The method similar_by_word() on a trained Word2Vec model returns the most semantically similar words to a given word and their similarity scores.
coverage_criteria: Student can write code to retrieve the top-5 similar words for 'car' using similar_by_word and interpret the results.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

anchors.locator: Example 7 – Palavras similares a car e house, page 201

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 7 on pages 200-201 uses similar_by_word to find words similar to 'car' and 'house', showing the cosine similarity scores.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Covers one method of the model; can be checked with a short coding exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Brown Corpus as a standard NLP dataset
before_phase4_candidates.description: The Brown Corpus is a collection of 500 English texts from 1961 containing over 1 million words, commonly used for NLP model training and evaluation.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the Brown Corpus (size, date, types of texts) and explain why it is a valuable resource for NLP.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 4 uses the Brown Corpus from NLTK, and page 199 describes its origin and size, noting its frequent use in NLP.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concept introduces a well-known dataset; can be assessed with a few factual questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec enables arithmetic with word vectors
before_phase4_candidates.description: Word2Vec represents words as vectors such that vector arithmetic like 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' ≈ 'queen' reflects semantic relationships.
coverage_criteria: Given a word vector equation, the student can identify the expected result word (e.g., king - man + woman = queen).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly demonstrates the math and explains how Word2Vec allows this.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is the fundamental capability that is demonstrated and can be tested with a simple analogy.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Words can be represented as feature vectors with numerical properties
before_phase4_candidates.description: A word can be encoded as a vector of numbers, where each dimension represents a semantic or descriptive feature such as authority, richness, gender, etc.
coverage_criteria: The student can describe that a word vector is a set of numbers representing properties, and give examples of possible features for a noun.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video walks through assigning numbers for authority, tail, rich, gender to words like 'king' and 'horse'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the concept of feature vectors is foundational before learning about learning them automatically.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Neural networks can learn word embeddings from a fake problem
before_phase4_candidates.description: Instead of hand-crafting features, word embeddings are learned as a side effect of training a neural network on an auxiliary task, like predicting a missing word.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain that the primary goal is to obtain word vectors, and the network is trained on a surrogate task such as filling in a blank.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

anchors.locator: [04:00] Learning Word Embeddings with Neural Networks

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explains taking a 'fake problem' (filling missing word) to learn embeddings as a side effect.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a key conceptual leap distinguishing manual feature engineering from learned embeddings.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Meaning of a word can be inferred from surrounding context
before_phase4_candidates.description: The context words around a missing word provide enough information to guess the missing word, illustrating distributional semantics.
coverage_criteria: Given a sentence with a blank, the student can use context to select the most appropriate word from options.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates with examples: 'eating ___ is very healthy' → apple/walnut; 'NASA launched ___' → rocket.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This principle underpins the training data generation and is a core linguistic insight.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Training data for Word2Vec is generated by sliding a window over text
before_phase4_candidates.description: By moving a fixed-size window across the text, we create input-output pairs: the context words (input) and the target word (output) to fill a blank.
coverage_criteria: Given a short text, the student can produce training samples using a window of size 3 or 5, identifying context and target words.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

anchors.locator: [07:41] Generating Training Samples for Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly generates training samples from a paragraph using a window of three words.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a concrete step in the Word2Vec pipeline, turning raw text into supervised training data.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec neural network uses one-hot encoded inputs and outputs
before_phase4_candidates.description: Words are converted to one-hot vectors of size equal to vocabulary, and the network learns to produce a probability distribution over the vocabulary as output.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain that each input word is a vector with a 1 at its index and 0s elsewhere, and the output layer has a softmax over all words.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes the input layer as one-hot encoded vectors of size 5000 for a vocabulary of 5000 words.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding the input/output representation is essential to understanding how the network processes text.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word embeddings are the learned weights between layers
before_phase4_candidates.description: In Word2Vec, the word vector for a word is the weight vector connecting its one-hot input to the hidden layer (or hidden to output, depending on architecture).
coverage_criteria: The student can indicate that after training, the embedding for a word is found in the weight matrix of the neural network.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly states: 'the word vector for king would be these weights w1 w2 w3 w4' and later for skip-gram the embedding is between input and hidden.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This demystifies how embeddings are actually obtained from the training process.

before_phase4_candidates.label: CBOW and Skip-Gram are two Word2Vec training techniques
before_phase4_candidates.description: Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) predicts the target word from context words; Skip-Gram predicts context words from the target word.
coverage_criteria: The student can distinguish between CBOW and Skip-gram based on the direction of prediction.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly contrasts the two: 'you have context... predict target' vs 'target and based on that we try to predict context'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: These are the two primary variants of Word2Vec, and understanding their difference is a key learning outcome.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec embeddings capture semantic and syntactic relationships
before_phase4_candidates.description: Learned vectors capture relationships like verb tenses (walking-walked), capital-country (Madrid-Spain), and analogies (king-queen).
coverage_criteria: The student can provide examples of relationships that word vectors can capture, such as gender, tense, or geography.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows visualizations of vector spaces revealing these relationships (male-female, verb tense, country-capital).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This highlights the practical power of Word2Vec and why it's useful.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec is a self-supervised learning approach
before_phase4_candidates.description: The training data (input-output pairs) is generated from the raw text itself without external labels, making it self-supervised.
coverage_criteria: The student can explain that Word2Vec does not require manually labeled data; the labels come from the text itself through the windowing process.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

anchors.locator: [07:41] Generating Training Samples for Word Embeddings

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions 'this problem is called self-supervised because all you had was this paragraph you did not have like X and Y' and you generate training samples.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Self-supervision is an important concept in machine learning, and Word2Vec is a classic example.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec analogy examples demonstrate compositional semantics
before_phase4_candidates.description: Analogies like 'USA - Washington D.C. + Delhi = India' show that vector offsets encode relational similarities.
coverage_criteria: The student can solve simple analogy tasks using vector arithmetic if given hypothetical embeddings.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: What is Word2Vec? A Simple Explanation

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video provides a quiz and shows analogies: USA-Washington+Delhi=India, Samsun-Galaxy+iPhone=Apple.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific application of vector arithmetic and tests comprehension of the concept.

before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Processando a Linguagem

anchors.locator: Livro: Mueller, John P. Aprendizado profundo para leigos.

extraction_reason.metadata_grounded_rationale: A referência ao livro 'Aprendizado profundo para leigos' e a aula pai sobre Word2Vec e redes neurais implicam que o estudo aborda aprendizado profundo, especificamente no contexto de linguagem. Mesmo que o título e a descrição não mencionem explicitamente aprendizado profundo, a referência bibliográfica e o contexto da aula tornam plausível a inclusão desse conceito como um sub-tópico do processamento de linguagem.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: É um conceito intermediário que conecta a técnica de redes neurais (vista em aulas anteriores) com aplicações em PLN. Não é excessivamente granular, pois é uma área de estudo estabelecida.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Word2Vec
before_phase4_candidates.description: Modelo de embeddings de palavras que representa palavras como vetores densos para capturar semântica.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve ser capaz de explicar o funcionamento básico do Word2Vec e sua utilidade em tarefas de PLN.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Processando a Linguagem

extraction_reason.metadata_grounded_rationale: Embora o título e a descrição do self-study não mencionem Word2Vec, a aula pai ('Word2Vec - Aplicação utilizando Redes Neurais') indica que este estudo é uma continuação que aplica Word2Vec. Portanto, o conceito Word2Vec é implicitamente coberto ou pré-requisito para este estudo. Como o self-study está diretamente ligado a essa aula, é defensável incluir Word2Vec como um candidato.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Word2Vec é um tópico específico, comumente ensinado em cursos de PLN e aprendizado profundo. É um conceito bem delimitado e ensinável.

reconciled_candidates.label: Vector Similarity using Distance and Nearest Neighbors
reconciled_candidates.description: How Euclidean distance quantifies vector similarity and how nearest neighbor search finds the closest items in a vector space.
coverage_criteria: Calculate Euclidean distance between two vectors.
Explain how a nearest neighbor search finds the closest item by comparing distances.
Implement a closest() function using Euclidean distance.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Euclidean distance and nearest neighbor search are interdependent; both describe vector similarity operations demonstrated together in the source.

reconciled_candidates.label: Solving Analogies with Vector Arithmetic
reconciled_candidates.description: Performing vector addition, subtraction, and averaging, and using these operations to solve analogies by vector differences.
coverage_criteria: Add and subtract vectors component-wise.
Given vectors for 'pink', 'red', 'blue', solve the analogy 'pink - red + blue = ?'.
Describe how vector difference captures semantic relationships.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Vector arithmetic operations are directly applied to solve analogies; both concepts form a single skill of using vector math for analogies.

reconciled_candidates.label: Distributional Hypothesis and Co-occurrence Word Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: The distributional hypothesis and building word vectors from co-occurrence counts to capture semantic similarity.
coverage_criteria: State the distributional hypothesis.
Given a small corpus, construct a simple co-occurrence matrix.
Explain why words with similar distributions yield similar vectors.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: The distributional hypothesis motivates co-occurrence vectors; they are inseparable in the source's progression from theory to practice.

reconciled_candidates.label: Dimensionality Reduction for Word Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: Applying dimensionality reduction to high-dimensional co-occurrence vectors to obtain compact word embeddings.
coverage_criteria: Explain why raw co-occurrence vectors can be redundant.
Name a technique for dimensionality reduction.
State typical embedding dimensions after reduction.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Concept stands alone as a distinct technique.

reconciled_candidates.label: Pre-trained GloVe Word Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: Using pre-trained GloVe vectors as 300-dimensional semantic representations of words.
coverage_criteria: Describe where GloVe vectors come from and their dimensionality.
Load GloVe vectors in spaCy.
Explain when to use pre-trained vectors.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Standalone concept on a specific pre-trained resource.

reconciled_candidates.label: Cosine Similarity for High-Dimensional Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: Using cosine similarity to measure the angle between vectors, suitable for high-dimensional spaces.
coverage_criteria: Define cosine similarity.
Given two vectors, compute their cosine similarity.
Explain why cosine similarity is preferred in high-dimensional spaces.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word Vector Arithmetic with Pre-trained Embeddings
reconciled_candidates.description: Applying arithmetic operations on pre-trained word embeddings to reveal semantic relationships.
coverage_criteria: Perform vector addition and subtraction with word embeddings.
Interpret the result of an arithmetic operation on word vectors.
Predict plausible results for operations like 'king - man + woman'.

reconciled_candidates.label: Sentence Similarity via Averaged Word Vectors
reconciled_candidates.description: Deriving sentence vectors by averaging word vectors and using them for sentence similarity.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to create a sentence vector from word vectors.
Compute the average of multiple word vectors.
Use cosine similarity to compare sentence vectors.

reconciled_candidates.label: Gensim Library and Text Preprocessing Pipeline
reconciled_candidates.description: Introduction to the Gensim library and its basic text preprocessing functions: tokenization, simple_preprocess, and Dictionary creation.
coverage_criteria: Describe Gensim's origin and purpose.
Use simple_preprocess() to tokenize text with parameters.
Create a Dictionary from tokenized documents.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates cover foundational Gensim setup and preprocessing; together they form the necessary first steps in a Gensim workflow.

reconciled_candidates.label: Dense vs Sparse Vector Representations
reconciled_candidates.description: Understanding the difference between dense and sparse vector representations in NLP.
coverage_criteria: Define dense and sparse vectors.
Give examples of when each is used in text representation.

reconciled_candidates.label: Training Word2Vec Models and Parameter Configuration
reconciled_candidates.description: Training word2vec embeddings with Gensim's Word2Vec class and configuring key parameters like size, window, sg, and training method.
coverage_criteria: Write code to instantiate Word2Vec with tokenized sentences.
Explain the meaning of at least three training parameters.
Choose appropriate parameters for a given training scenario.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Training Word2Vec and configuring its parameters are two sides of the same process; they are blended in the source's tutorial.

reconciled_candidates.label: Saving and Loading Word2Vec Models
reconciled_candidates.description: Persisting and reloading trained Word2Vec models using Gensim's save and load functions.
coverage_criteria: Write code to save a trained model to disk.
Load a saved model and use it for inference.

reconciled_candidates.label: Using Pre-trained Word2Vec Models for Similarity Queries
reconciled_candidates.description: How to load pre-trained word embeddings with gensim.downloader and find semantically similar words using similar_by_word.
coverage_criteria: Write code to load a pre-trained model (e.g., word2vec-google-news-300) and retrieve top-5 similar words for a given word.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates describe practical code operations for loading and querying pre-trained embeddings; together they form the skill of using pre-trained models.

reconciled_candidates.label: Semantic Word Vectors and Analogies
reconciled_candidates.description: Word2Vec represents words as dense vectors that capture semantic and syntactic relationships, enabling arithmetic-based analogies such as king - man + woman ≈ queen.
coverage_criteria: Explain how words as feature vectors allow arithmetic, and solve simple analogy tasks like capital-country relationships.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates all convey the core idea that word vectors are semantically meaningful and support analogies through vector arithmetic, from introduction to specific examples.

reconciled_candidates.label: Self-Supervised Context-Based Embedding Learning
reconciled_candidates.description: Word2Vec learns embeddings by training a neural network on a self-supervised task: predict a target word from its surrounding context using a sliding window to generate training pairs.
coverage_criteria: Describe the process of creating training data with a context window, and explain that the network learns to fill in missing words, yielding word embeddings as a side effect.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates describe the training data generation, the use of context to infer meaning, the 'fake problem' paradigm, and the self-supervised nature, which together form the learning mechanism.

reconciled_candidates.label: Word2Vec Neural Network Architecture
reconciled_candidates.description: The Word2Vec model uses one-hot encoded inputs and learns embeddings as the weights between layers, which can be extracted after training.
coverage_criteria: Explain the input and output representations (one-hot vectors) and identify where word embeddings are stored in the network.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Both candidates detail the neural network structure: input encoding and the location of learned embeddings.

reconciled_candidates.label: CBOW and Skip-Gram Architectures
reconciled_candidates.description: Word2Vec has two training variants: CBOW predicts the target word from context, while Skip-Gram predicts context words from the target.
coverage_criteria: Distinguish between CBOW and Skip-Gram based on prediction direction.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: A single candidate covering the key distinction between the two Word2Vec training approaches.

candidate_snapshot.label: Brown Corpus as a standard NLP dataset
candidate_snapshot.description: The Brown Corpus is a collection of 500 English texts from 1961 containing over 1 million words, commonly used for NLP model training and evaluation.
coverage_criteria: Student can describe the Brown Corpus (size, date, types of texts) and explain why it is a valuable resource for NLP.
candidate_snapshot.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - utilizando word embeddings em Python

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: Example 4 uses the Brown Corpus from NLTK, and page 199 describes its origin and size, noting its frequent use in NLP.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Concept introduces a well-known dataset; can be assessed with a few factual questions.

coverage_criteria: O aluno deve ser capaz de explicar os conceitos básicos de PLN e identificar aplicações de análise de sentimentos.

anchors.locator: Processando a Linguagem no contexto de análise de sentimentos.

extraction_reason.metadata_grounded_rationale: O título 'Processando a Linguagem' e a descrição mencionam explicitamente processamento de linguagem no contexto de análise de sentimentos. Essas são evidências diretas de que o conteúdo aborda PLN e análise de sentimentos.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Conceito amplo, porém é o mais específico que a metadata permite sem adivinhar sub-tópicos. Posteriormente pode ser refinado com mais evidências.

coverage_criteria: O aluno deve ser capaz de aplicar modelos simples para classificar sentimentos em amostras de texto.

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Conceito bem definido e comumente ensinado como um tópico independente dentro de PLN. É um candidato natural dado o contexto.
